title: Map Scale Ratio from Distances: Recover 1:n
description: Recover a map's 1:n scale ratio from a measured map distance and its true ground distance with Map Scale Ratio from Distances. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a runway that measures 4.2 cm on an unlabelled sheet and runs 2.1 km on the ground gives 210,000 ÷ 4.2 = 50,000 — the sheet is a 1:50,000 map, whatever its legend forgot to say.
quick_answer: Map Scale Ratio from Distances recovers a map's scale ratio from two matched measurements: a distance measured on the map and the same distance's true length on the ground. Enter both and read the 1:n ratio — the identification every unlabelled sheet, shrunken photocopy and mystery screenshot eventually needs.
steps_intro: Two measurements of the same thing; the ratio between them is the scale:

body.t: Screenshots crop legends away. One known feature — a runway, a lake, a surveyed road — restores the scale the crop removed, and the
Copiers rescale silently. Measuring a known distance exposes the true effective ratio, which is the only one measurements on that sheet may use.
A sheet claims 1:25,000. Trust but verify: one feature check confirms the claim or reprices every measurement you were about to take from it.
Old sheets state scales in dead units or not at all. A feature that still exists — a church-to-bridge distance — ties the antique to the modern ratio system.

Runways are ideal: exactly documented lengths, dead straight, visible on everything. 4.2 cm on paper against 2.1 km true gives 1:50,000 — and the check takes one feature because a true map has one scale everywhere.

A photograph of a map, or a screenshot in perspective, has no single scale — near and far edges disagree. Two features at opposite ends returning different ratios is the signature of distortion, and the honest response is to abandon the sheet for measurement.

rows: Relative measurement error shrinks as the feature grows
The ratio is unitless — 2.1 km must meet 4.2 cm as 210,000 cm
Sheets are printed at standard ratios — 1:49,700 measured is a 1:50,000 sheet plus your ruler's honesty
popular_table.note: Ground truth for the feature can come from a second, trusted source: a distance computed between its endpoints with the coordinate tools here, an official length, or a surveyed record.

faq: What if my two features disagree?
The sheet has no single scale — perspective, distortion or a locally stretched scan. Report both ratios with their features, and do not measure the sheet for anything that matters.
Can I use a screen image's pixels?
Yes — pixels are a unit like centimetres if the ground length is known and the image is a flat, undistorted map render. Perspective photos of screens fail the same test paper does.
How precise is the recovered ratio?
As precise as your shorter measurement. A 4.2 cm feature read to ±0.05 cm gives roughly ±1% — plenty to identify the standard scale the sheet was printed at.
The ratio is not a round number.
Round to the nearest standard scale for identification, but keep the measured ratio for calculations on that particular (possibly rescaled) sheet — both facts are yours to use.
Compute it between the feature's endpoints with the distance tools here, or take a documented length (runways publish theirs). The ratio inherits that source's accuracy.
Not at sheet scales: a printed map already projects the ground, and the ratio describes the sheet. Continental wall maps are the exception that cartographers, not ratios, handle.
Any recovered 1:n converts to words ('one inch to…') through the Map Unit Converter — the ratio is the canonical form the others derive from.
